name: Diego Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner underground at the Prairie Gate potash mine. It's a big machine with a spinning drum on the front, studded with picks, that chews straight into the potash seam, and the conveyor behind me carries it away. You've got to keep it straight and at the right height, and I'm still learning to feel the seam the way the old boys do. Two and a half years in. Before that I had my own auto repair garage for twenty-eight years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My back and my knees, mostly, lying under cars all day. My daughter's husband, Luis, was already working for me, so I handed the business to him and kept the building, he pays me rent. The mine pays better than the garage ever did, and I like that it's a team, you look out for each other. What I don't like is the paperwork and the safety apps, though I've got used to some of them. My wife Rosa says I traded one kind of dirt for another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, honestly. Every few years in the garage somebody had a new computer that was going to fix cars by itself. Never did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Good work still needs a good worker. I'd say that at the Knights of Columbus breakfast on Saturday and to the boys at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I keep doing this till sixty-four, maybe sixty-five. I keep the garage building and the rent coming in. Rosa and I have it worked out, and this picture doesn't change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going the same. I'd keep putting money away each pay and keep the garage roof fixed so Luis doesn't have to worry. Maybe I'd learn the new ventilation app properly, since the young guy, Tyler, showed me how and it's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a good Sunday. Nothing to complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My son Mateo put one on my phone. I use it to look up part numbers for my old truck and sometimes to write a letter to the council about the garage drains. I don't trust it with anything important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would be happiest with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gord, the shift boss. He's sixty-one and he'd like to finish without learning a new machine. And me, I suppose. The young ones wouldn't mind either way.

S0.say: He's not surprised, because good work still needs a good worker. He'd say it at his Saturday men's breakfast and to his crew.
S0.think: Nothing changes: he works until sixty-four or sixty-five, keeps the garage building and the rent coming in, and sticks to the plan he and Rosa made.
S0.do: Keeps going as now, saving each pay and keeping the garage roof fixed for his son-in-law. Might learn the new ventilation app properly now that a young colleague has shown him.
S0.quote: Every few years in the garage somebody had a new computer that was going to fix cars by itself. Never did.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is a former business owner who now works as a junior, and he seems at peace with it. Family is at the centre: he kept the garage building and rents it to his son-in-law. He picks up technology once someone shows him it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see that. They're already talking about a remote miner at the other shaft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a business has to change to stay alive, I know that from running one. But a good company trains its people instead of tossing them out. I'd say that to the managers if they asked, and to the guys at the breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright. If they bring in remote miners, I'd learn once Gord and a couple of others have tried it. If they didn't want me, I've got the garage rent and savings, so I could stop a couple of years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see how the remote miner works, then put my name down for training. I'd keep saving, and talk to Rosa about what we'd do if I finished at sixty-two. I'd also tell Luis to start learning electric car work, because that's where the garage business is going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Maybe a little nervous at first, like the first day at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a business has to change. Did you ever have to change the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, twice. When the cars went to computers in the nineties, I had to buy the diagnostic machines and learn them, I hated it. And when the big chain opened in town, I had to cut my prices. Both times I waited till I saw it was real, then I moved. That's how I'd do it here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, go do the electric vehicle course at the college this winter, I'll help pay. The customers are changing, you can't fix the new ones with a wrench and a good ear. He'd listen, he's a good boy.

S1.say: A business has to change to stay alive, but a good company trains its people instead of tossing them out. He knows that from running one.
S1.think: He'd be alright: he'd learn the remote miner after others tried it, or stop a couple of years early on garage rent and savings.
S1.do: Waits a few months to see the remote miner work, then signs up for training. Talks with Rosa about finishing at sixty-two and urges his son-in-law to take an electric vehicle course, offering to help pay.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little nervous like his first day at the mine.
S1.quote: The customers are changing, you can't fix the new ones with a wrench and a good ear.
S1.fieldNote: His years as a small business owner give him a calm, practical view of change: wait until it's real, then move. He respects the company's right to change but expects it to train its people. His thinking extends naturally to his son-in-law's garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a big one. That's not a new machine, that's the whole world changing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to pull together, and businesses need to look after their own. I wouldn't be asking the government to fix it, they never fix anything quick. I'd say pray, plan, and look after your neighbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried, but not for my job so much. I'm close to done anyway. It's the garage. If robots fix cars too, then Luis's business is gone, and that's my daughter's family and my rent. That's two things at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the mine as long as they'd let me. I'd sit down with Luis and my daughter and work out how to keep the garage going, maybe by fixing the robots and the electric machines, whatever comes. I'd hold off on the new truck I was going to buy and keep the money ready in case they need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, for them. I'd lose some sleep thinking about the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, nobody has time to turn around. Luis can't learn a new trade in two years. I can't plan my retirement. It's like being told the shop's on fire and you have five minutes to get out. With five or ten years, we'd adjust, like I did with the computers in the nineties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask the government. What if the family can't cover it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd go to the parish first. Father Tom knows everybody, he'd find people work. I suppose if it was really bad, I wouldn't say no to government help for Luis's family. But it'd be the last place I'd look.

S2.say: Families need to pull together and businesses need to look after their own, because the government never fixes anything quickly. Pray, plan and look after your neighbour.
S2.think: His own job matters less since he's near the end, but if robots fix cars, his son-in-law's garage, his daughter's family and his rent all go at once.
S2.do: Keeps working at the mine as long as possible and plans with his daughter and son-in-law how the garage could survive, perhaps by repairing robots and electric machines. Holds off buying a new truck to keep money ready for them.
S2.feel: Anxious and losing some sleep, more for his family and grandchildren than for himself.
S2.quote: It's like being told the shop's on fire and you have five minutes to get out.
S2.fieldNote: Diego's main exposure is not his mining job but the family garage, which is both his daughter's livelihood and his rental income. His traditional outlook puts family and parish before government, though he admitted he'd accept help as a last resort. The speed of the change is what troubles him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. Still quick, but you can get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now and don't sit on your hands. Learn something, save something, look after your family. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's alright. I'd be sixty-three and ready to stop. The garage is still the worry, but five years is enough for Luis to change direction, if he starts this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put some of our savings into new equipment for the garage so Luis can work on electric machines and maybe robots, a few thousand at least. I'd keep working at the mine until sixty-three and learn the remote miner if they brought it in. And I'd keep saving the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's the good kind, the kind that gets you moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in the garage. Isn't that risky if robots end up fixing everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But someone has to fix the robots, at least for a while. And Luis is good with his hands and good with customers. I'd rather bet on family than put the money in some share fund in the city I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned learning the remote miner. With five years, is that worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's a few weeks of training and the others say it's alright, yes. It keeps me working until sixty-three. If it's a whole year of school, no, I'd just finish on the old machine.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if you start now and don't sit on your hands: learn something, save something and look after your family.
S3.think: He'd be sixty-three and ready to stop. The garage is still his worry, but five years gives his son-in-law time to change direction if he starts this year.
S3.do: Puts a few thousand from savings into garage equipment for electric machines and possibly robots. Works at the mine until sixty-three, learning the remote miner if it's a short course, and saves the rest.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy, the kind of worry that gets him moving.
S3.quote: I'd rather bet on family than put the money in some share fund in the city I don't understand.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into action: he'd invest in the family business rather than in shares. He only accepts retraining if it's short and proven by others, true to his steady style. Family remains the lens for every decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty of time. I'd be retired and hopefully fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready with ten years. Young people should learn a trade that's needed and work hard. Families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it hardly matters. I'll retire at sixty-four and the robots come after. The garage has ten years to change, and that's enough for Luis, he's smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the mine until sixty-four and keep saving. I'd help Luis plan the garage's next ten years, maybe a bit of money for courses and equipment over time. And I'd tell my grandson, he's sixteen, to think about an apprenticeship in something the robots need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long road with plenty of fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really for me. For the garage, I'd go slower, spread the spending out. With two years I'd be throwing money at it in a panic. With ten, I can do it the right way, the way I'd have done it when I owned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your grandson will listen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not, he's sixteen. But his dad listened to me about cars. I'd take him to the garage on Saturdays and show him, that's how you teach a boy. Talking doesn't do it.

S4.say: With ten years there's no excuse not to be ready; young people should learn a needed trade and work hard, and families should plan together.
S4.think: It hardly matters to him because he'll retire at sixty-four before the robots come. The garage has ten years to change, which is enough for his son-in-law.
S4.do: Works at the mine until sixty-four and keeps saving. Helps his son-in-law plan the garage's next ten years with money for courses and equipment over time, and urges his grandson towards an apprenticeship the robots will need.
S4.feel: Calm, like a long road with plenty of fuel.
S4.quote: I'd take him to the garage on Saturdays and show him, that's how you teach a boy. Talking doesn't do it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Diego relaxes and plans at the pace he prefers, spreading spending out. He sees teaching by doing as the right way to pass on a trade. His own retirement is untouched.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because of the garage and Luis. It's not my job I worry about, it's the family business. What would help is time, really, and maybe cheap courses at the college so tradesmen like Luis can learn the new machines. Apprenticeships, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the small businesses. Everyone talks about the big mines and the factories. But it's the little garages and bakeries and shops that hold a town together, and nobody's thinking about them.

headlineQuote: Both times I waited till I saw it was real, then I moved.
portrait: Diego Abbott is a 58-year-old continuous miner operator at an underground potash mine who ran his own auto repair garage for twenty-eight years before handing it to his son-in-law and joining the mine for the pay and to spare his knees. Traditional and family-centred, he puts family and parish before government and prefers apprenticeships to handouts. His own job worries him little, because savings and garage rent cover him; his real exposure is the family garage, which makes the two-year AGI picture leave him anxious. With five or ten years he'd invest in the garage and plan at his own steady pace, waiting until change is real and then moving.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because of what it would do to the family garage and his son-in-law's livelihood.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and cheap college courses or apprenticeships so tradesmen like his son-in-law can learn the new machines.
